cards.title: Unconditional SAT time lower bounds
cards.formal: Can one prove an unconditional time lower bound for Boolean satisfiability on a general computation model, without an additional workspace restriction? The source discusses both proving an exponential dependence on the number of variables and the much smaller milestone of ruling out linear time. It does not select one machine model, representation and quantitative endpoint for this card. The recovered scope is explained below; the entry remains a formulation requiring specification.
cards.why: An unconditional lower bound for satisfiability would establish a limitation of general computation for a central natural problem, beyond limitations of a solver family or consequences of a conjecture. Even a modest bound is significant when it applies without an extra memory restriction. Its precise computational model is part of the mathematical achievement.

The source asks for unconditional time lower bounds on general computation models.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation. A conjunctive normal form formula is an AND of clauses, each clause being an OR of literals. CNF-SAT asks whether there is an assignment satisfying every clause. General CNF-SAT permits unbounded clause width; \(k\)-CNF-SAT restricts every clause to at most the fixed integer \(k\) literals.

Circuit-SAT instead receives a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input variables, AND, OR and NOT gates, and a designated output gate, and asks whether some input assignment makes that output 1. These problems are polynomially interreducible, but an arbitrary polynomial increase in input length cannot be ignored in a linear-time or precise exponential-time claim.

The number \(n\) of variables differs from the full input bit length \(L\). An explicit CNF encoding includes every literal occurrence, its variable index, sign and clause separators. A circuit encoding includes gate descriptions and wire endpoints. A bound in \(n\) alone must specify how formula or circuit size may grow with \(n\), or separately account for input-reading and polynomial factors in \(L\). Statements about linear time in \(L\), linear time in the number of machine words, and linear time in \(n\) are not interchangeable.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has a fixed finite program, alphabet and number of tapes; each step accesses a constant number of tape cells and moves each head by at most one cell. A random-access model instead permits addressed memory access. A word-RAM typically stores words of \(O(\log L)\) bits and charges unit cost for a specified list of arithmetic, Boolean, shift and memory operations. The instruction list, word length and treatment of larger integers affect fine time bounds. The source’s phrase “robust model” does not itself fix these details.

A worst-case time bound requires one uniform algorithm to halt and give the correct satisfiability answer on every valid input within that bound. For a randomized version, correctness probability and whether time is worst-case or expected must additionally be fixed. No oracle or nonuniform advice is implicit.

For a selected encoding and model, excluding \(O(L)\) time means that no constant \(C\) and correct algorithm have running time at most \(CL\) on every sufficiently long valid input. A specified lower bound such as \(\Omega(L^{1+\varepsilon})\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) is stronger than merely excluding linear time. Likewise, excluding \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(L)\) time and excluding every \((2-\varepsilon)^{n}\operatorname{poly}(L)\) algorithm are different exponential claims. These are examples of possible endpoints, not a replacement conjecture selected by this review.

An unconditional lower bound uses no assumption such as \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), the Exponential Time Hypothesis or the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. It may still be a theorem only about a restricted class of algorithms. In particular, a time-space tradeoff rules out satisfying a time bound and a separate workspace bound simultaneously. It does not rule out an algorithm with the same running time that uses more workspace. “Unrestricted space” here means no extra workspace promise beyond what the running time itself permits.
cards.answer_criterion: First specify one SAT variant, explicit encoding and input measure, computational model, randomness convention and quantitative time claim. Then give a proof of that claim without a conjectural complexity assumption, or a matching algorithm that refutes it. A restricted-space theorem, a lower bound for another complete problem, or a conditional fine-grained reduction does not meet an unrestricted SAT time target.

context_blocks.title: The source names a research program and two different scales
context_blocks.text: The introduction asks whether the exponential dependence of exhaustive search can be proved inherent on a robust model. It then emphasizes that even excluding linear-time SAT remains beyond the unrestricted lower bounds discussed there. Treating both remarks as one fully quantified conjecture would conflate distinct targets.

context_blocks.title: Resource restrictions are part of existing theorems
context_blocks.text: The time-space literature proves lower bounds for general random-access machines while limiting their workspace. Fortnow, Lipton, van Melkebeek and Viglas explicitly require simultaneous time and space bounds in their theorem. The significance of using a general machine does not remove the workspace condition.

context_blocks.title: A recent time lower bound concerns other languages
context_blocks.text: Williams’s simulation theorem places time \(t\) on multitape Turing machines inside space \(O(\sqrt{t\log t})\). Its consequences include languages decidable in linear space that require almost quadratic time on that model. Corollary 1.3 identifies a space-bounded machine-acceptance language; it does not identify SAT as that hard language.

context_blocks.title: The recent model distinction also matters
context_blocks.text: The checked simulation report explicitly leaves extension to arbitrary random-access computation unresolved, while discussing an oblivious-access special case. The 2026 journal abstract retains the multitape Turing-machine result. Thus it neither supplies a general RAM lower bound nor fills the missing SAT-specific target in this card.

cards.context:
The introduction asks whether the exponential dependence of exhaustive search can be proved inherent on a robust model. It then emphasizes that even excluding linear-time SAT remains beyond the unrestricted lower bounds discussed there. Treating both remarks as one fully quantified conjecture would conflate distinct targets.

The time-space literature proves lower bounds for general random-access machines while limiting their workspace. Fortnow, Lipton, van Melkebeek and Viglas explicitly require simultaneous time and space bounds in their theorem. The significance of using a general machine does not remove the workspace condition.

Williams’s simulation theorem places time \(t\) on multitape Turing machines inside space \(O(\sqrt{t\log t})\). Its consequences include languages decidable in linear space that require almost quadratic time on that model. Corollary 1.3 identifies a space-bounded machine-acceptance language; it does not identify SAT as that hard language.

The checked simulation report explicitly leaves extension to arbitrary random-access computation unresolved, while discussing an oblivious-access special case. The 2026 journal abstract retains the multitape Turing-machine result. Thus it neither supplies a general RAM lower bound nor fills the missing SAT-specific target in this card.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
